### 38.912 Shared `resolve_path()` Still Allows Workspace Escapes Via Lexical Absolute Paths And Symlinks

**Status**: Not started  
**Priority**: P1

| Issue | File | Detail |
|-------|------|--------|
| The shared workspace path guard still treats lexical prefixes as sufficient containment, so absolute paths like `/workspace/../tmp/x` and in-workspace symlinks can make file tools operate outside the workspace root | `generation/g5d/src/tools/mod.rs:254`, `generation/g5d/src/tools/mod.rs:257`, `generation/g5d/src/tools/mod.rs:260`, `generation/g5d/src/tools/mod.rs:274`, `generation/g5d/src/tools/mod.rs:304`, `generation/g5d/src/tools/file_ops.rs:171`, `generation/g5d/src/tools/file_ops.rs:291`, `generation/g5d/src/tools/file_ops.rs:411`, `generation/g5d/src/tools/file_ops.rs:559`, `generation/g5d/src/tools/file_ops.rs:661`, `generation/g5d/src/tools/interface.rs:1474` | `resolve_path()` is the common guard for `read_file`, `write_file`, `edit_file_replace`, `delete_file`, `list_directory`, and `extract_interface`, but it never canonicalizes the final target. In the absolute-path branch it only checks `path.starts_with(workspace_path)`, and Rust's path-prefix check is lexical, so a path like `/workspace/../tmp/secret.txt` still passes even though it resolves outside the workspace. In the relative-path branch, `..` segments are normalized away, but symlink targets are not: a repo-controlled symlink such as `workspace/link -> /etc` yields a resolved path under the workspace prefix while later file I/O follows the symlink to the external target. The result is that the helper enforcing the tool boundary can still approve out-of-workspace reads, writes, deletes, listings, and interface extraction against arbitrary accessible files. |

**Desired cleanup**:

- Canonicalize or otherwise `realpath`-style resolve the final target before the
  containment check, in both the absolute and relative branches.
- Reject paths whose canonical target leaves the workspace root, including
  symlink traversals and lexical absolute paths containing `..`.
- Add regression coverage for `/workspace/../...` inputs and for symlinked
  external targets across the file and interface tool surfaces.

### 38.913 `git_pull` Still Rewrites The Checkout Without Any Draft Or Dirty-Tree Guard

**Status**: Not started  
**Priority**: P1

| Issue | File | Detail |
|-------|------|--------|
| The agent `git_pull` path still bypasses the CRDT flush/clean invariants used by the other mutating git tools, then force-refreshes the worktree, so local draft or shell edits can be lost under a successful pull | `generation/g5d/src/tools/git_ops.rs:408`, `generation/g5d/src/tools/git_ops.rs:440`, `generation/g5d/src/tools/mod.rs:435`, `generation/g5d/src/tools/mod.rs:440`, `generation/g5-common/src/ops/merge.rs:113`, `generation/g5-common/src/ops/merge.rs:128`, `generation/g5-common/src/ops/merge.rs:133`, `generation/g5-common/src/ops/merge.rs:141`, `generation/g5-common/src/ops/merge.rs:152`, `generation/g5-common/src/git/repo.rs:525` | `GitCommitTool` explicitly flushes the CRDT peer and blocks on failed materializations before mutating git state, but `GitPullTool` has no `crdt_peer` at all and is registered without one. It immediately resolves the current branch and calls `ops::pull(...)`. The shared pull helper then fast-forwards or rebases and finishes by `checkout_branch(...)` plus `checkout_head_force()`, which forcibly rewrites the working tree to match the new HEAD. There is no preflight dirty-file check and no draft-state protection in this path. So if the workspace has unflushed CRDT edits or ordinary uncommitted terminal changes, a successful `git_pull` can overwrite them while still returning a normal success message like `Fast-forwarded ...` or `Rebased ...`. This is a real data-loss path, not just a stale-read issue. |

**Desired cleanup**:

- Give `GitPullTool` the same CRDT flush and clean-materialization guard used by
  `GitCommitTool` before any branch mutation happens.
- Refuse pull/rebase when the working tree or draft state is dirty instead of
  forcing the checkout through.
- Add coverage proving `git_pull` fails closed in the presence of unflushed
  draft changes or local uncommitted edits.

### 38.921 `detect_fs_changes()` Still Never Propagates File Deletions

**Status**: Not started  
**Priority**: P2

| Issue | File | Detail |
|-------|------|--------|
| The live out-of-band CRDT change detector still only walks currently existing files and only ever enqueues writes, so shell-side deletes never become CRDT deletions | `generation/g5d/src/crdt/mod.rs:420`, `generation/g5d/src/crdt/mod.rs:447`, `generation/g5d/src/crdt/mod.rs:485`, `generation/g5d/src/crdt/materialize.rs:247`, `generation/g5d/src/crdt/materialize.rs:250` | `detect_fs_changes()` builds `entries` from the current filesystem tree and then loops only over those paths. For changed files it calls `enqueue_file_write_with_author(...)`, but there is no second pass that compares `materializer.known_file_states()` or `known_file_hashes` against missing paths. The incremental materializer already has explicit delete behavior when a dirty path has no CRDT content, but the out-of-band detector never emits such a deletion signal. So a terminal-side `rm`, build cleanup, or generator that removes a file can leave the CRDT document, remote peers, and reconnect state still thinking the file exists. In the worst case a later materialization from stale CRDT state can recreate a file the shell already deleted. |

**Desired cleanup**:

- Teach `detect_fs_changes()` to diff the known-state path set against the
  current filesystem and emit CRDT deletions for disappeared files.
- Keep delete propagation symmetrical with create/modify propagation so shell
  side effects cannot leave stale files alive in the shared draft state.
- Add regression coverage proving an out-of-band `rm` is reflected to peers and
  does not get resurrected on reconnect/materialization.

### 38.922 Out-Of-Band CRDT Change Detection Still Follows Symlinked Paths Outside The Workspace

**Status**: Not started  
**Priority**: P1

| Issue | File | Detail |
|-------|------|--------|
| The shipped out-of-band change scanner still classifies entries with `path.is_dir()` / `path.is_file()`, so a symlink inside the workspace can make the worker read and sync external file contents as though they were ordinary workspace files | `generation/g5d/src/crdt/mod.rs:439`, `generation/g5d/src/crdt/mod.rs:448`, `generation/g5d/src/crdt/mod.rs:462`, `generation/g5d/src/crdt/mod.rs:487`, `generation/g5d/src/crdt/mod.rs:801`, `generation/g5d/src/crdt/mod.rs:832`, `generation/g5d/src/crdt/mod.rs:836`, `generation/g5d/src/crdt/mod.rs:837` | `walkdir_collect()` recurses based on `path.is_dir()` / `path.is_file()`, which follow symlinks. That means a workspace symlink like `vendor-link -> /private/vendor` is treated as a normal directory tree and its target files are returned as entries rooted under the workspace symlink path. `detect_fs_changes()` then successfully `strip_prefix()`es those lexical paths against the workspace root, reads the target bytes with `tokio::fs::read(&entry_path)`, and enqueues them into CRDT under a relative path like `vendor-link/secret.txt`. **Desired cleanup**:

- Use symlink-aware metadata (`symlink_metadata()` / `DirEntry::file_type()`)
  when walking the workspace for out-of-band change detection.
- Refuse to recurse into or read symlink targets unless their canonical target
  is still inside the workspace root.
- Add regression coverage proving a workspace symlink cannot leak external file
  contents into CRDT change propagation.

  out-of-band and conflict-accept paths.

  losslessly or rejected with a clear error instead of being silently mangled.

### 38.929 Case-Insensitive Search Still Reports Unicode Match Columns From A Lowercased Surrogate String
**Status**: ✅ FIXED (synced from `BATCH_PLAN.md`, 2026-04-28)

**Priority**: P2

| Issue | File | Detail |
|-------|------|--------|
| The shared search engine still computes case-insensitive match columns from `line.to_lowercase()`, so Unicode matches can get column offsets that do not point at the real location in the original line | `generation/g5d/src/search/mod.rs:58`, `generation/g5d/src/search/mod.rs:65`, `generation/g5d/src/search/mod.rs:531`, `generation/g5d/src/search/mod.rs:546`, `generation/g5d/src/search/mod.rs:547`, `generation/g5d/src/search/mod.rs:550`, `generation/g5d/src/search/mod.rs:551`, `generation/g5d/src/search/mod.rs:553`, `generation/g5d/src/tools/search.rs:82`, `generation/g5d/src/tools/search.rs:97`, `generation/g5d/src/tools/search.rs:99` | `SearchMatch.column` is documented as the 0-based column offset of the match start. But the case-insensitive matcher lowercases the entire line, finds offsets in that transformed string, and returns those positions unchanged. For Unicode text, lowercasing can change the number of code points or UTF-8 bytes compared with the original line, so the offset in `line_lower` is not guaranteed to be the offset in `line`. The live `semantic_search` tool then prints and returns those columns as if they were authoritative. That means jump-to-match, highlighting, or any downstream consumer of the reported column can point at the wrong place for perfectly valid non-ASCII content. |

**Desired cleanup**:

- Compute case-insensitive matches in a way that preserves offsets back to the
  original line, or explicitly document and enforce an ASCII-only contract.
- Keep the `SearchMatch.column` contract honest across the engine and the tool
  surface that prints `path:line:column`.
- Add regression coverage with Unicode case-folding examples that would change
  string length under `to_lowercase()`.

**Status**: Not started

That works only while lowercasing preserves byte lengths and positions. For Unicode text, `to_lowercase()` can change the number of bytes or code points, so the match position in `content_lower` is not guaranteed to point at the same place in `content`. The function later snaps to char boundaries, but it never remaps the offset back to the original string. **Desired cleanup**:

  searched for, even under Unicode case folding.

| The WebSocket flush path still drains the entire outbound queue before sending, and on the first send error it just `break`s, so the unsent tail of the batch is lost permanently | `generation/g5d/src/crdt/sync.rs:937`, `generation/g5d/src/crdt/sync.rs:943`, `generation/g5d/src/crdt/sync.rs:947`, `generation/g5d/src/crdt/sync.rs:948`, `generation/g5d/src/crdt/sync.rs:958`, `generation/g5d/src/crdt/sync.rs:960`, `generation/g5d/src/crdt/sync.rs:961`, `generation/g5d/src/crdt/sync.rs:962` | `flush_outbound_ws()` removes every queued delta up front and decrements the byte counter before any network send happens. There is no requeue of the failed delta, no requeue of the unsent remainder, and no forced reconnect/full-sync marker. **Desired cleanup**:

  plus full-state resync, rather than a warn-and-drop path.

**Desired cleanup**:

  when the materializer lacks a trustworthy baseline for that path.

  starts immediately after a write burst.

| A successful `write_file` still does not seed either read tracker, so the next `edit_file_replace` on that same path can be rejected as if the agent never read the file it just wrote | `generation/g5d/src/tools/file_ops.rs:307`, `generation/g5d/src/tools/file_ops.rs:315`, `generation/g5d/src/tools/file_ops.rs:436`, `generation/g5d/src/tools/file_ops.rs:439`, `generation/g5d/src/crdt/mod.rs:392`, `generation/g5d/src/crdt/mod.rs:394`, `generation/g5d/src/crdt/mod.rs:408`, `generation/g5d/src/crdt/attribution.rs:165`, `generation/g5d/src/crdt/attribution.rs:186`, `generation/g5d/src/crdt/attribution.rs:221`, `generation/g5d/src/crdt/attribution.rs:224` | `write_file` writes the file and enqueues a CRDT full-write, which records authorship hunks via `record_full_write(...)`. But it never updates `FileReadTracker` and never calls `crdt_peer.record_read(...)`. The next `edit_file_replace` consults `has_been_modified_since_read(...)`, which treats “no prior read” as modified, and then falls into `validate_edit(...)`. `AttributionTracker::validate_edit()` rejects any file whose `last_read_at` is still `None`, even if the only prior writer was the same agent via `write_file`. So a perfectly normal workflow of “create/overwrite a file, then refine one exact string in it” still fails unless the agent performs a redundant `read_file` in between. |

**Desired cleanup**:

- Treat a successful agent-authored `write_file` as satisfying the read-before-
  edit precondition for that exact resulting content.
- Keep the file-level read tracker and CRDT attribution tracker aligned so
  follow-on edit tools behave consistently after a successful write.
- Add coverage proving `write_file` followed by `edit_file_replace` on the same
  path does not require an unnecessary intervening `read_file`.

### 38.966 `edit_file_replace` And `edit_spec_replace` Still Accept Empty `old_string`

**Status**: Not started  
**Priority**: P2

| Issue | File | Detail |
|-------|------|--------|
| The replace-style edit tools still treat `old_string = ""` as a valid exact-match request, so malformed calls silently prepend `new_string` instead of failing validation | `generation/g5d/src/tools/file_ops.rs:400`, `generation/g5d/src/tools/file_ops.rs:449`, `generation/g5d/src/tools/file_ops.rs:466`, `generation/g5d/src/tools/spec_ops.rs:615`, `generation/g5d/src/tools/spec_ops.rs:640`, `generation/g5d/src/tools/spec_ops.rs:648` | Both tools only validate that `old_string` is present and is a string. They never require it to be non-empty. In `edit_file_replace`, `text.matches(old_string).count()` with `old_string = ""` returns a positive count, so the “not found” guard is bypassed and `replacen("", new_string, 1)` inserts `new_string` at the start of the file. `edit_spec_replace` is even simpler: `content.contains("")` is always true, so it also falls straight into `replacen("", new_string, 1)` and prepends text to the spec. That means a malformed or schema-bypassing call can perform a real mutation while claiming to have replaced an “exact string,” which is a broken tool contract distinct from the already-tracked multi-match ambiguity issue. |

**Desired cleanup**:

- Reject empty `old_string` values at the tool boundary for both file and spec
  replace tools.
- Keep “replace exact string” semantics strict so malformed inputs cannot
  degrade into prepend mutations.
- Add coverage proving `old_string = ""` returns a validation/tool error
  instead of modifying the target content.

### 38.967 File Mutation Tools Still Return Error After The Local Mutation Already Happened

**Status**: Not started

|-------|------|--------|

Only afterward does it attempt `crdt_peer.enqueue_file_write(...)`. If that enqueue fails, the tool returns an error result describing the CRDT problem. That is more honest than the already-tracked spec/view false-success path, but it still leaves a contract trap: callers who interpret `ToolResult::error` as “the requested mutation did not happen” can retry and end up double-writing content, hitting `String not found` on the second edit, or getting a `NotFound` delete on a file already removed locally. The local workspace and the tool’s success/error surface are therefore still split-brain under CRDT enqueue failure. |

**Desired cleanup**:

- Either make these mutations transactional with respect to CRDT enqueue, or
  return a result shape that clearly distinguishes “local mutation applied” from
  “authoritative sync failed.”
- Keep retry semantics safe so a second attempt cannot blindly reapply or
  mis-handle a mutation that already changed the local checkout.
- Add coverage proving enqueue failures do not leave the caller guessing whether
  the file was changed, edited, or deleted locally.

### 38.968 `edit_file_replace` Still Lossily Rewrites Non-UTF-8, NUL-Free Files

**Status**: Not started  
**Priority**: P2

| Issue | File | Detail |
|-------|------|--------|
| The file-read/edit path still classifies “binary” only by NUL-byte presence and then uses `String::from_utf8_lossy()`, so non-UTF-8 files without NUL bytes can be shown and rewritten with replacement characters | `generation/g5d/src/tools/file_ops.rs:85`, `generation/g5d/src/tools/file_ops.rs:87`, `generation/g5d/src/tools/file_ops.rs:192`, `generation/g5d/src/tools/file_ops.rs:200`, `generation/g5d/src/tools/file_ops.rs:432`, `generation/g5d/src/tools/file_ops.rs:466`, `generation/g5d/src/tools/file_ops.rs:469` | `read_file` rejects a file as binary only when the first 8KB contains a `\\0` byte. Files that are non-UTF-8 but NUL-free therefore pass through to `String::from_utf8_lossy(...)`, which replaces invalid byte sequences with `U+FFFD`. `edit_file_replace` uses that same lossy decode and then writes the full `new_content` string back to disk as UTF-8. So a malformed or merely legacy-encoded file can be silently normalized into replacement characters even when the requested replacement touched only an ASCII substring. This is separate from the already-tracked CRDT-side lossy sync bug: the standalone file tool itself can corrupt bytes before collaborative sync is even considered. |

**Desired cleanup**:

- Use real UTF-8 validation instead of NUL-byte heuristics for deciding whether
  `read_file` / `edit_file_replace` can safely operate as text tools.
- Fail closed on non-UTF-8 file content rather than round-tripping it through
  `from_utf8_lossy()` and rewriting corrupted bytes.
- Add coverage proving non-UTF-8, NUL-free files are rejected or preserved
  faithfully instead of being rewritten with replacement characters.

### 38.973 `CrdtPeer::disconnect()` Still Returns Before The Background Sync Task Has Actually Stopped
**Status**: ✅ FIXED (synced from `BATCH_PLAN.md`, 2026-04-28)

**Priority**: P2

| Issue | File | Detail |
|-------|------|--------|
| The CRDT disconnect path still reports success after sending shutdown signals, but it has no join/ack path for the spawned sync loop, so the background task can keep running after `disconnect()` returns | `generation/g5d/src/crdt/mod.rs:693`, `generation/g5d/src/crdt/mod.rs:700`, `generation/g5d/src/crdt/mod.rs:705`, `generation/g5d/src/crdt/sync.rs:81`, `generation/g5d/src/crdt/sync.rs:83`, `generation/g5d/src/crdt/sync.rs:214`, `generation/g5d/src/crdt/sync.rs:215`, `generation/g5d/src/crdt/sync.rs:326`, `generation/g5d/src/crdt/sync.rs:327`, `generation/g5d/src/crdt/sync.rs:330`, `generation/g5d/src/crdt/sync.rs:331`, `generation/g5d/src/crdt/sync.rs:332`, `generation/g5d/src/crdt/sync.rs:435` | `SyncEngine::start()` fire-and-forgets the main loop with `tokio::spawn(...)` and returns a `SyncHandle` that exposes only `control_tx`; there is no join handle or completion notification. `CrdtPeer::disconnect()` therefore just sends `Shutdown` and then calls `engine.stop()`, which marks the engine disconnected but does not wait for the spawned task to finish. On the reconnect path, the background loop can even be sitting inside `sleep(backoff_ms).await` and only drains `control_rx.try_recv()` after the sleep completes. So `disconnect()` can return while the sync task is still alive, possibly for up to the current reconnect backoff window, leaving teardown races and lingering background activity behind a false-clean shutdown result. |

**Desired cleanup**:

- Return a shutdown acknowledgment or join the spawned sync task so
  `disconnect()` only succeeds once the background loop has actually exited.
- Make reconnect backoff shutdown-responsive instead of waiting for the next
  sleep boundary before noticing `Shutdown`.
- Add coverage proving disconnect does not return while the spawned sync loop is
  still running.

### 38.989 Inbound CRDT Materialization Still Holds The Document Mutex Across Disk I/O

**Status**: Not started

But the same mutex is also needed for normal sync and tool flows: `PullNow` encodes a state vector under `doc.lock()`, inbound WebSocket updates call `d.apply_update(...)` under that lock, and local writes enqueue CRDT updates by calling `doc.set_text(...)` while holding it. **Desired cleanup**:

  progress while inbound materialization is performing slow file operations.
- Add coverage or instrumentation proving large inbound writes do not stall
  unrelated CRDT operations behind the document mutex.

### 38.991 `CrdtPeer` Reconnect Still Consumes Its Inbound Materialization Channel On First Connect

**Status**: Not started  
**Priority**: P2

| Issue | File | Detail |
|-------|------|--------|
| A `disconnect()` → `connect()` cycle on the same CRDT peer can come back without any live inbound materialization path, because both sides of that channel are one-shot `take()`s consumed on the first connection | `generation/g5d/src/crdt/mod.rs:203`, `generation/g5d/src/crdt/mod.rs:243`, `generation/g5d/src/crdt/mod.rs:247`, `generation/g5d/src/crdt/mod.rs:693`, `generation/g5d/src/crdt/mod.rs:705`, `generation/g5d/src/crdt/sync.rs:195`, `generation/g5d/src/crdt/sync.rs:208`, `generation/g5d/src/crdt/sync.rs:678`, `generation/g5d/src/crdt/sync.rs:681`, `generation/g5d/src/crdt/sync.rs:682` | `CrdtPeer::connect()` permanently takes the inbound materializer receiver via `inbound_materialize_rx()`, and `SyncEngine::start()` permanently takes the sender via `self.inbound_tx.take()`.   peer still has a real path from inbound update to on-disk materialization.

  materializes later inbound updates to disk.

|-------|------|--------|
| The spec-listing tool still accepts every `*.md` file under the chosen specs directory as an ontology entry, even if it has no spec frontmatter or is just an incidental note/readme | `generation/g5d/src/tools/spec_ops.rs:786`, `generation/g5d/src/tools/spec_ops.rs:790`, `generation/g5d/src/tools/spec_ops.rs:794`, `generation/g5d/src/tools/spec_ops.rs:800`, `generation/g5d/src/tools/spec_ops.rs:802`, `generation/g5d/src/tools/spec_ops.rs:817` | `list_specs` only checks that a walked file ends in `.md`. **Desired cleanup**:

- Keep incidental notes/readmes out of the ontology inventory so agents do not

It resolves the path and immediately calls `tokio::fs::remove_file(...)`, then mirrors the deletion into CRDT. So deletion currently sidesteps the product's core human-authority invariant: a model can remove an unread or human-updated file outright even though a smaller in-file edit on the same path would have been vetoed. **Desired cleanup**:

### 38.1017 Task Completion Still Persists The Sentinel `"no-changes"` As A Real Commit SHA
**Status**: ✅ FIXED (synced from `BATCH_PLAN.md`, 2026-04-28)

**Priority**: P1

| Issue | File | Detail |
|-------|------|--------|
| The completion path still uses the literal string `"no-changes"` as a no-op sentinel and then forwards it through the normal `commitSha` field, so branch-backed task completion can stamp `"no-changes"` into `jobs.head_commit` and `tasks.base_commit` as though it were a real git revision | `generation/g5d/src/tools/task_lifecycle.rs:431`, `generation/g5d/src/tools/task_lifecycle.rs:433`, `generation/g5d/src/tools/task_lifecycle.rs:435`, `generation/g5d/src/tools/task_lifecycle.rs:487`, `generation/g5d/src/tools/task_lifecycle.rs:693`, `generation/g5d/src/worker/lifecycle.rs:325`, `generation/g5d/src/worker/lifecycle.rs:330`, `generation/g5d/src/worker/lifecycle.rs:339`, `generation/g5-api/src/services/task_service.rs:2349`, `generation/g5-api/src/services/task_service.rs:2388`, `generation/g5-api/src/services/task_service.rs:2415`, `generation/g5-api/src/services/task_service.rs:2433` | `task_lifecycle` returns `"no-changes"` when `ops::checkpoint()` reports no commit, and `report_completion()` serializes that value into the internal `commitSha` field exactly like a real SHA. The worker lifecycle uses the same sentinel in its checkpoint metadata. On the API side, `transition_task()` only checks whether `commit_sha` is present; for branch-backed jobs it stages `completion_head_advance = (old_head, commit_sha)` and then writes that `commit_sha` into both `jobs.head_commit` and the task row's `base_commit` during the completed transition. There is no special handling or validation that distinguishes the sentinel from an actual revision. The result is a real branch-state corruption path: a no-op completion can poison persisted branch metadata with the string `"no-changes"`, and every downstream diff, merge, and head-resolution path now has to cope with a non-SHA branch head. |

**Desired cleanup**:

- Keep no-op completions distinct from real commit SHAs all the way through the
  worker/tool/API boundary.

  metadata instead of persisting `"no-changes"`.

### 38.1018 `run_in_terminal` Still Lies About Defaulting `cwd` To The Workspace Root
**Status**: ✅ FIXED (synced from `BATCH_PLAN.md`, 2026-04-28)

**Priority**: P2

| Issue | File | Detail |
|-------|------|--------|
| The tool schema still says omitted `cwd` defaults to the workspace root, but reused terminal sessions actually run in whatever directory the persistent shell was already left in | `generation/g5d/src/tools/terminal.rs:109`, `generation/g5d/src/tools/terminal.rs:145`, `generation/g5d/src/tools/terminal.rs:200`, `generation/g5d/src/terminal/mod.rs:181`, `generation/g5d/src/terminal/mod.rs:197`, `generation/g5d/src/terminal/mod.rs:224`, `generation/g5d/src/terminal/mod.rs:437`, `generation/g5d/src/terminal/session.rs:322`, `generation/g5d/src/terminal/session.rs:342`, `generation/g5d/src/terminal/session.rs:355` | `run_in_terminal` advertises `cwd` as “Working directory (defaults to workspace root),” and brand-new PTY sessions do start at `workspace_path`. But the default execution path is to reuse the last active session. In that reused-session case, `TerminalManager::execute()` forwards `cwd = None`, and `TerminalSession::execute_command()` only prepends `cd {dir} && ...` when a `cwd` is explicitly supplied. Otherwise it writes the command directly into the already-running shell. So after any earlier call that used a different `cwd` or manually ran `cd ...`, the next call with no `cwd` does not reset to the workspace root at all; it inherits the shell's lingering directory state. That makes the published tool contract false and creates a subtle behavior bug where later terminal commands can run against the wrong subtree even though the caller followed the documented default. |

**Desired cleanup**:

- Either make omitted `cwd` explicitly reset the shell to the workspace root on
  every call, or document and expose the real “current terminal directory”
  semantics instead of claiming a root default.
- Keep the PTY path and isolation-backed `exec_command` path aligned on the same
  working-directory contract.
- Add coverage proving reused no-`cwd` terminal calls cannot silently drift away
  from the workspace root unless the caller asked for that behavior.

### 38.1038 `PATCH /comments/:id` Still Treats An Empty Body As A False-Success Mutation

**Status**: Not started  
**Priority**: P3

| Issue | File | Detail |
|-------|------|--------|
| The comment update route still accepts `{}` / all-null bodies, returns `200 OK`, and bumps `updated_at` even though neither content nor resolution changed | `generation/g5-api/src/routes/comments.rs:100`, `generation/g5-api/src/routes/comments.rs:487`, `generation/g5-api/src/routes/comments.rs:504`, `generation/g5-api/src/services/comment_service.rs:61`, `generation/g5-api/src/services/comment_service.rs:745`, `generation/g5-api/src/services/comment_service.rs:794`, `generation/g5-api/src/services/comment_service.rs:801` | `UpdateCommentRequest` makes both `content` and `resolved` optional, and the route documents the endpoint as a partial update. But `CommentService::update_comment()` never checks that at least one field is present. Its SQL always runs `UPDATE comment_index ... updated_at = now()` and uses `COALESCE($2, content)` / `COALESCE($3, resolved)` to leave the other fields unchanged. That makes accidental empty updates look like successful edits, and it can also distort any workflow that treats `updated_at` as meaningful activity, including deleted-branch retention where GC is keyed off `updated_at`. |

**Desired cleanup**:

- Require at least one mutable field in `UpdateCommentRequest` before running
  the update query.
- Return a validation error for empty/all-null bodies instead of mutating only
  `updated_at`.
- Add coverage proving empty comment-patch payloads cannot round-trip as
  successful updates.

Later, task assignment threads `job_row.created_by` into both `resolve_task_secrets(...)` and `resolve_task_scm_credentials(...)`, and `ConfigService::resolve_effective()` only merges the user scope when that argument is present. The result is that user-triggered background work can silently lose the caller's personal `llm.apiKey`, custom secrets, and per-user model/provider overrides. This diverges from the adjacent good paths: normal `POST /jobs` and create-view jobs both preserve `Some(user_id)`. In practice, a user whose org/workspace defaults are incomplete can watch view sync or first-time repo uplift get accepted and then fail on the worker under a different effective config than the one their other interactive actions use. |

**Desired cleanup**:

- Thread the authenticated user through every public job-creation path that is
  meant to run on that user's effective runtime config, including `sync_view`
  and add-repo uplift bootstrap.
- Add regression coverage proving user-scoped config and secrets are visible in
  task assignment for these flows just like ordinary create-job and create-view
  paths.
- Audit other fire-and-forget job creation sites for the same `created_by =
  NULL` drift before more user-scoped runtime behavior lands.

| Both resolve routes still call `orchestrate_post_resolution(...)` even when `resolve_escalation()` explicitly reports `transitioned = false`, so stale duplicate resolves can re-run unblock/resume side effects against an already-resolved escalation | `generation/g5-api/src/services/human_escalation_service.rs:349`, `generation/g5-api/src/routes/human_escalations.rs:338`, `generation/g5-api/src/routes/human_escalations.rs:347`, `generation/g5-api/src/routes/internal.rs:2267`, `generation/g5-api/src/routes/internal.rs:2275`, `generation/g5-api/src/routes/internal.rs:2574` | `HumanEscalationService::resolve_escalation()` is intentionally idempotent: if the escalation is already `resolved`, it returns the existing row with `transitioned: false` and skips the state update. Today that helper still attempts task unblocking, and the surrounding debt already shows it is meant to grow into the job/task resume path. So a stale retry against an already-resolved escalation can still re-run execution-side effects even though the service contract said no transition happened. Once unblock/resume is fully wired, duplicate resolve calls will be able to poke execution state again through a path that claims to be idempotent. |

**Desired cleanup**:

  WebSocket emission.
- Gate `orchestrate_post_resolution(...)` behind the same transition check so

- Add idempotency coverage proving repeated resolve calls do not re-run unblock,
  resume, or other orchestration side effects.

| The worker-only escalation create/resolve/cancel/context routes still scope only by org match, so any same-org worker that learns another task or escalation UUID can mutate or read that other task’s escalation state without owning the task lease | `generation/g5-api/src/routes/internal.rs:2129`, `generation/g5-api/src/routes/internal.rs:2171`, `generation/g5-api/src/routes/internal.rs:2223`, `generation/g5-api/src/routes/internal.rs:2289`, `generation/g5-api/src/routes/internal.rs:2337`, `generation/g5-api/src/routes/internal.rs:2377`, `generation/g5-api/src/db/scoped.rs:315`, `generation/g5-api/src/db/scoped.rs:323`, `generation/g5-api/src/routes/internal.rs:987`, `generation/g5-api/src/routes/internal.rs:996` | The internal escalation routes all derive an authoritative `org_id` from the target task/job/escalation and then open `scoped_db_for_org(...)`. For worker JWTs that helper only checks `auth_org_id == org_id` and then returns an unscoped DB handle; it does not prove the caller owns the task. The same file already has the stronger pattern in `report_usage()`, where `load_worker_task_context(...)` plus `require_task_owner(...)` reject same-org spoofing before touching task-linked state. The escalation endpoints never apply that guard. So a worker running task A can create a fake escalation on task B, resolve or cancel B’s existing escalation, return it to human review, or read B’s resolved escalation context, as long as both tasks live in the same org. That breaks task-level isolation inside the worker control plane and lets one worker interfere with another task’s human-gating workflow. |

**Desired cleanup**:

- Require the same task-ownership check for escalation routes that other
  task-linked internal mutation paths already use.
- For escalation-id routes, resolve the task first and then prove the caller
  owns that task before allowing read/write access.
- Add negative coverage proving a same-org worker cannot create, resolve,
  cancel, reroute, or read escalation context for another task’s escalation.

**Desired cleanup**:

### 38.1094 Explicit Org Switch Still Leaves The Shared `current-user` Query Stale
**Status**: ✅ FIXED (synced from `BATCH_PLAN.md`, 2026-04-28)

**Priority**: P2

| Issue | File | Detail |
|-------|------|--------|

But the React Query hooks that much of the settings/org UI actually consumes are separate. `useCurrentUser()` and `useOrgs()` both cache `/api/v1/users/me` under the fixed `['current-user']` key with a 5-minute `staleTime`, and `switchOrg()` never calls `queryClient.invalidateQueries()` or `setQueryData()` for that cache. `UserSettingsPanel` reads those hooks directly to resolve `activeOrg` and org-scoped capabilities. So after an explicit org switch, the app can end up in a split-brain state where JWT-backed auth context has moved to the new org while settings/org surfaces continue rendering the previous org list, role, or selected org metadata until some later refetch happens. This is distinct from the already-documented periodic-refresh staleness: it happens on the explicit switch path that is supposed to be the freshness fix. |

**Desired cleanup**:

- Treat `switchOrg()` as a full session-sync path by updating or invalidating the
  shared `['current-user']` query at the same time it updates `AuthContext.user`.
- Avoid maintaining two independent “current user” sources that can drift after
  one org switch succeeds.
- Add org-switch coverage proving settings/org consumers backed by
  `useCurrentUser()` / `useOrgs()` immediately reflect the new org context
  without waiting for a later refetch window.

But `AuditedRouter::exempt_route()` means “authenticated only,” not “must have one of these scopes,” and several sensitive user routes still live there: `GET/PATCH /api/v1/users/me`, `GET/POST /api/v1/orgs`, `GET /api/v1/orgs/:orgId`, `GET /api/v1/orgs/:orgId/members`, and invitation accept/decline. The result is a scope-boundary bypass: a zero-scope PAT, or a narrowly scoped PAT that should only read one surface, can still exercise every authenticated-only route that relies on identity but not explicit scope checks. That means PAT scopes are not the true authority boundary the feature implies, and callers can do more than the token contract suggests. |

**Desired cleanup**:

  authenticated-only routes instead of treating PAT scopes as advisory.

  profile/org/invitation routes whose behavior exceeds the token's declared
  scope set.

It does not re-select from current memberships or verify that the stored org is still the best active context. `resolve_effective_scopes()` then quietly returns `Vec::new()` when that stored org is nil or no longer matches a membership, but `mint_jwt()` still uses the stale `target_org_id` in the JWT claims. That creates session drift in both directions: users who first logged in with no orgs can keep refreshing into nil-org / zero-scope JWTs after they later gain or create an org, and users removed from the stored org can keep receiving JWTs whose `org` claim points at that departed org while their effective scopes collapse to empty. **Desired cleanup**:

- Re-resolve the active org from current memberships on refresh whenever the
  caller does not explicitly request a target org.

  membership.

  org membership removed” so the default refresh flow cannot strand users in

| The public escalation list is exposed as a page/per-page API, but the underlying query still pages with `LIMIT/OFFSET` on `ORDER BY created_at DESC` alone, so rows that share the same timestamp can move across page boundaries between requests | `generation/g5-api/src/routes/human_escalations.rs:233`, `generation/g5-api/src/routes/human_escalations.rs:256`, `generation/g5-api/src/services/human_escalation_service.rs:508`, `generation/g5-api/src/services/human_escalation_service.rs:529` | `GET /api/v1/escalations` explicitly documents `page` / `perPage` pagination and returns paginated metadata, but `HumanEscalationService::list_escalations()` sorts only by `created_at DESC` before applying `LIMIT` and `OFFSET`. When two escalations land in the same timestamp bucket, Postgres is free to return those ties in either order on different reads. That makes later pages unstable: a refetch can duplicate an escalation that was already seen on page N or skip one that should have appeared on page N+1. The product already treats escalation lists as live data, so this is a real contract gap for any consumer that pages beyond the default first screen. |

  as `id DESC`, or move the list to cursor/keyset pagination.

**Status**: Not started

| Issue | File | Detail |
|-------|------|--------|
| When OAuth login auto-accepts more than one pending invitation in the same transaction, the first session still chooses its active org with `ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 1`, which is unstable because all of those newly inserted membership rows share the same default timestamp | `generation/g5-api/src/services/auth_service.rs:831`, `generation/g5-api/src/services/auth_service.rs:846`, `generation/g5-api/src/services/auth_service.rs:850`, `generation/g5-api/src/services/auth_service.rs:893`, `generation/g5-api/src/services/auth_service.rs:899`, `generation/g5-api/src/db/migrations/001_initial_schema.sql:42`, `generation/g5-api/src/db/migrations/001_initial_schema.sql:47` | `handle_callback()` auto-accepts every pending invitation matching the login email by inserting one `org_memberships` row per invitation inside a single transaction, then it picks the active org for the fresh JWT/refresh token with `SELECT org_id ... ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 1`. But `org_memberships.created_at` is just `DEFAULT now()`. In Postgres that timestamp is transaction-stable, so multiple memberships inserted during the same login transaction receive the same `created_at` value. The final `ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 1` therefore has no deterministic tie-breaker and can choose any of the simultaneously accepted orgs as the user's first active session. This is distinct from the already-documented client-side active-org ambiguity: here the backend auth/session state itself is nondeterministic before the browser even renders. A newly invited user who belongs to multiple orgs on first login can therefore land in a seemingly random org, with the refresh token pinned to that arbitrary choice. |

**Desired cleanup**:

- Stop deriving the initial active org from a bare timestamp sort when multiple
  memberships can be created in the same transaction.
- Choose a deterministic policy for multi-invite first login, such as the
  invitation explicitly accepted, a stable org-id/order tie-break, or an
  explicit “choose org” handoff before minting the first org-scoped session.
- Add login coverage proving users with multiple pending invitations get a
  deterministic initial org instead of whichever membership row Postgres
  happens to return first.

### 38.1112 Initial Auth Bootstrap Still Accepts A JWT-Only Session Even When Profile Load Fails

**Status**: Not started  
**Priority**: P2

| Issue | File | Detail |
|-------|------|--------|
| Initial auth bootstrap still installs a bearer JWT and decoded scopes before it proves `/api/v1/users/me` can load, so a profile-fetch failure leaves the browser looking logged out while authenticated API state remains active | `generation/client/src/hooks/useAuth.tsx:103`, `generation/client/src/hooks/useAuth.tsx:130`, `generation/client/src/hooks/useAuth.tsx:152`, `generation/client/src/hooks/useAuth.tsx:257`, `generation/client/src/hooks/useAuth.tsx:261`, `generation/client/src/hooks/useAuth.tsx:271`, `generation/client/src/hooks/useAuth.tsx:279`, `generation/client/src/hooks/useAuth.tsx:455` | `initialAuth()` calls `refreshToken()` first, and that helper short-circuits to the locally stored JWT whenever `g5_auth_token` exists and is still unexpired. As soon as a JWT comes back, the bootstrap path writes it into `jwtRef`, installs it into the shared API client with `setApiToken(jwt)`, and decodes scopes into auth state before it calls `fetchCurrentUser(jwt)`. If `/api/v1/users/me` then returns non-OK or throws, `fetchCurrentUser()` just returns `null`. The bootstrap path does not clear the token, clear scopes, or force logout in that case; it simply leaves `user` unset and flips `isLoading` to `false`. `RequireAuth` therefore redirects the UI to the public unauthenticated surface because `!user`, even though the tab still has a live bearer token and scope set installed for subsequent API calls. This creates a split-brain startup state where the app can look logged out while still acting authenticated until the token expires or the user explicitly logs out. That is distinct from the already-tracked explicit-org-switch partial-success path because it happens on cold bootstrap before any switch action. |

**Desired cleanup**:

- Treat initial auth bootstrap as atomic: do not install or retain a session
  JWT in client auth state unless `/api/v1/users/me` succeeds.
- If the profile load fails after refresh succeeds, clear the token/scopes and
  surface a real auth failure instead of leaving a hidden authenticated session
  behind.
- Add client auth coverage proving bootstrap cannot end in `user = null` while
  the shared API client still carries an active bearer token.

### 38.1113 Permission Replacement APIs Still Turn Duplicate Scope Lists Into Generic 500s

**Status**: Not started  
**Priority**: P2

| Issue | File | Detail |
|-------|------|--------|
| The full-replacement permissions APIs validate only that scope strings exist, not that the submitted list is unique, so duplicate scope entries hit table uniqueness constraints and bubble out as generic server errors | `generation/g5-api/src/routes/permissions.rs:96`, `generation/g5-api/src/routes/permissions.rs:104`, `generation/g5-api/src/routes/permissions.rs:115`, `generation/g5-api/src/services/permission_service.rs:357`, `generation/g5-api/src/services/permission_service.rs:443`, `generation/g5-api/src/services/permission_service.rs:539`, `generation/g5-api/src/services/permission_service.rs:626`, `generation/g5-api/src/db/migrations/001_initial_schema.sql:717`, `generation/g5-api/src/db/migrations/001_initial_schema.sql:724`, `generation/g5-api/src/db/migrations/001_initial_schema.sql:736` | `SetOrgScopesRequest`, `SetUserScopesRequest`, and `SetWorkspaceOverrideRequest` all accept `Vec<String>` bodies, and `PermissionService::validate_scopes()` only checks that each supplied string exists in `oauth_scopes`. The three replacement methods then delete existing rows and re-insert every submitted scope exactly as provided. But the underlying tables all enforce uniqueness (`PRIMARY KEY (org_id, scope)`, `UNIQUE (org_id, user_id, scope)`, `UNIQUE (workspace_id, user_id, scope)`). So payloads like `{"scopes":["workspaces:read","workspaces:read"]}` survive validation and then die on the second insert with a SQL uniqueness error. The transaction rolls back, but the caller gets a backend failure instead of a clean validation response explaining that duplicate scopes are invalid input. Because these endpoints are explicitly “full replacement” APIs, clients reasonably expect set semantics; today the contract still treats duplicate list items as a server fault. |

**Desired cleanup**:

- Reject duplicate scope entries at the request-validation boundary, or
  normalize the input to a deduplicated set before writing.
- Return a validation error that points at the duplicated scope values instead
  of surfacing a raw uniqueness failure as a 500.
- Add endpoint coverage proving all three replacement APIs handle duplicate
  scope lists deterministically.

The schema also allows this: `user_scope_grants` and `workspace_permission_overrides` only foreign-key `users`, `orgs`, and `workspaces`, not membership rows. That means an admin can seed scope rows for any existing user UUID, including users outside the org or outside an invite-only workspace. **Desired cleanup**:

  target org or workspace at the time of the write.

**Status**: Not started

| The full-replacement permission routes still never verify that the target org, user, or workspace exists before they mutate rows, so bad IDs return a fake success when `scopes` is empty and a generic foreign-key 500 when `scopes` is non-empty | `generation/g5-api/src/routes/permissions.rs:390`, `generation/g5-api/src/routes/permissions.rs:457`, `generation/g5-api/src/routes/permissions.rs:549`, `generation/g5-api/src/services/permission_service.rs:357`, `generation/g5-api/src/services/permission_service.rs:443`, `generation/g5-api/src/services/permission_service.rs:539`, `generation/g5-api/src/db/migrations/001_initial_schema.sql:717`, `generation/g5-api/src/db/migrations/001_initial_schema.sql:724`, `generation/g5-api/src/db/migrations/001_initial_schema.sql:736` | `set_org_default_scopes()`, `set_user_scopes()`, and `set_workspace_override()` all implement the same pattern: validate scope strings, `DELETE` existing rows for the supplied path ids, then `INSERT` one row per scope. None of those service methods first proves that the target org, user, or workspace actually exists as a valid management target. That creates payload-dependent behavior. If the caller submits `scopes: []`, only the `DELETE` runs, so the route returns `200 OK` with an empty result even when the target `userId` or `workspaceId` never existed. If the caller submits any real scopes, the first `INSERT` falls through to a foreign-key violation on `org_default_scopes`, `user_scope_grants`, or `workspace_permission_overrides`, which surfaces as a generic server failure rather than a 404/validation error. The contract is therefore unstable in exactly the wrong way: the same bad target id can look like a clean success or an internal crash depending only on whether the replacement set is empty. |

**Desired cleanup**:

- Preflight the target org/user/workspace and return a structured not-found or
  validation error before any delete/insert work begins.

  path-targeted admin mutations.
- Add endpoint coverage proving bad target ids are rejected consistently for
  both empty and non-empty replacement payloads.

### 38.1125 OAuth Auto-Accept Still Consumes Pending Invitations Even When The Invited Role Was Not Applied

**Status**: Not started  
**Priority**: P2

| Issue | File | Detail |
|-------|------|--------|
| The OAuth login auto-accept path still marks each pending invitation `accepted` even when the membership insert was skipped by `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`, so a stale or raced invite can disappear without ever applying its invited role | `generation/g5-api/src/services/auth_service.rs:846`, `generation/g5-api/src/services/auth_service.rs:850`, `generation/g5-api/src/services/auth_service.rs:852`, `generation/g5-api/src/services/auth_service.rs:864`, `generation/g5-api/src/services/auth_service.rs:868`, `generation/g5-api/src/db/migrations/001_initial_schema.sql:42`, `generation/g5-api/src/db/migrations/001_initial_schema.sql:48` | Inside `handle_callback()`, OAuth login auto-accepts pending org invitations by first attempting `INSERT INTO org_memberships ... ON CONFLICT (org_id, user_id) DO NOTHING`, then unconditionally updating the invitation row to `status = 'accepted'`. Because `org_memberships` is keyed by `(org_id, user_id)`, the insert can be a no-op whenever another path has already created that membership, for example after a race with another acceptance flow or any stale pending invite that now points at an already-added member. In that case the invitation is still consumed and shown as accepted even though its `role` was never written onto the membership row. The product effect is silent role loss: an admin can believe an invited `admin` or `viewer` role was accepted through login, while the user keeps whatever membership role they already had and the pending invitation is no longer available to inspect or retry. This is distinct from the already-documented race/500 paths on explicit invitation acceptance; here the login path fails soft and reports success. |

**Desired cleanup**:

- Do not mark a pending invitation accepted unless the login path can prove the
  intended membership state now matches the invitation's role.
- When the membership row already exists with a different role, return or log a
  structured conflict instead of silently consuming the invitation.
- Add OAuth-login coverage proving stale or raced pending invitations cannot be
  marked accepted while leaving the user's org role unchanged.

| The shared event-websocket bootstrap still sends whatever bearer is in memory to `/api/v1/auth/ws-ticket` and gives up on any non-OK response, even though the client already has a JWT refresh-and-retry path for CRDT ticketing | `generation/client/src/App.tsx:398`, `generation/client/src/App.tsx:404`, `generation/client/src/App.tsx:407`, `generation/client/src/App.tsx:412`, `generation/client/src/lib/crdt.ts:312`, `generation/client/src/lib/crdt.ts:338`, `generation/client/src/lib/crdt.ts:348`, `generation/client/src/lib/crdt.ts:372`, `generation/client/src/lib/crdt.ts:377`, `generation/client/src/lib/ws.ts:275`, `generation/client/src/lib/ws.ts:279`, `generation/client/src/lib/ws.ts:852` | `AppRoutes.getWsTicket()` reads the current API token with `getApiToken()`, posts it once to `/api/v1/auth/ws-ticket`, and returns `""` on any non-OK response. There is no preflight expiry check, no `refreshJwt()` attempt, and no one-shot retry on `401`/`403`. By contrast, the CRDT client already does exactly that before giving up: it inspects the JWT expiry, calls `refreshJwt()` when the token is stale, and retries the ticket request once after auth failures. So the product has two different recovery behaviors for the same short-lived ws-ticket flow. After a tab sits open long enough for the in-memory bearer to expire, the app-wide event socket can fall straight into the already-documented empty-token reconnect loop instead of refreshing the session and recovering the way CRDT does. Users see notifications, task updates, and other workspace events stay disconnected until a full page auth refresh, even though the client already contains a working stale-JWT recovery pattern elsewhere. |

**Desired cleanup**:

- Reuse the CRDT ticket-refresh flow for the shared event websocket so both
  realtime channels recover from stale JWTs the same way.
- Treat `401`/`403` from `/api/v1/auth/ws-ticket` as an auth-refresh boundary
  before falling into reconnect backoff.
- Add browser coverage proving an expired bearer can recover event websocket
  connectivity without a full page reload.

The returned branch detail therefore carries `head_commit = 000000...` for every normal add-repo success path, not just for invalid branches. The route then hands that zero SHA back to the client and later skips local branch materialization entirely because `materialize_workspace_branch_refs()` ignores zero heads. **Desired cleanup**:

  the branch as tracking until the repo has actually been materialized.

  the add-repo response.

  fake zero head commit.

**Status**: ✅ FIXED (synced from `BATCH_PLAN.md`, 2026-04-28)

| The public create-session flow still lets callers send `scopeType = "task"` without any `scopeRef`, which persists a row that claims to be task-scoped but has `task_id = NULL`; downstream attach then still returns success against that malformed session | `generation/g5-api/src/routes/chat.rs:136`, `generation/g5-api/src/routes/chat.rs:562`, `generation/g5-api/src/services/chat_service.rs:478`, `generation/g5-api/src/services/chat_service.rs:482`, `generation/g5-api/src/services/chat_service.rs:504`, `generation/g5-api/src/services/chat_service.rs:1433`, `generation/g5-api/src/routes/chat.rs:1123`, `generation/g5-api/src/db/migrations/001_initial_schema.sql:517` | `CreateSessionRequestDTO` makes `scopeRef` optional. In `ChatService::create_session()`, the `scope_type == "task"` branch only parses `scope_ref` when it exists; otherwise it quietly leaves `task_id = None` and still inserts the row with the caller-supplied `scope_type`. There is no database invariant requiring task-scoped sessions to carry a task id. That means a direct API caller can mint a session like `(session_type = 'task', scope_type = 'task', task_id = NULL, scope_ref = NULL)`. Later, `attach_session()` validates only `session.session_type == "task"` and returns a normal success payload with `taskId = null` and `crdtDocId = null`. **Desired cleanup**:

  `task_id = NULL` and that attach rejects malformed task sessions.

**Status**: ✅ FIXED (synced from `BATCH_PLAN.md`, 2026-04-28)

**Priority**: P3

|-------|------|--------|
| The browser PAT editor models scopes as a deduplicated toggle set, but the backend still persists duplicate `scopes` array entries verbatim, so direct callers can create keys with repeated scope badges and non-canonical auth claims | `generation/client/src/components/settings/OrgCredentialManager.tsx:120`, `generation/client/src/components/settings/OrgCredentialManager.tsx:298`, `generation/g5-api/src/services/api_key_service.rs:116`, `generation/g5-api/src/services/api_key_service.rs:135`, `generation/g5-api/src/services/api_key_service.rs:183`, `generation/g5-api/src/services/api_key_service.rs:273`, `generation/g5-api/src/db/migrations/040_api_keys.sql:13` | `toggleApiScope()` adds or removes one scope at a time from a React array, so the shipped UI behaves like a set and cannot submit duplicates.   stored rows, list responses, or auth claims.

### 38.1167 `stop_generation` Still Ignores The Zero-Row Race And Can Report A False Stop

**Status**: Not started  
**Priority**: P2

| Issue | File | Detail |
|-------|------|--------|
| The public chat stop route still returns `stopped: true` and emits `chat.done` even when the guarded `UPDATE ... WHERE status IN ('streaming','pending')` matched no rows, so a racing completion can turn stop into a false-success acknowledgement | `generation/g5-api/src/services/chat_service.rs:826`, `generation/g5-api/src/services/chat_service.rs:837`, `generation/g5-api/src/services/chat_service.rs:850`, `generation/g5-api/src/routes/chat.rs:908` | `ChatService::stop_generation()` first loads the message and verifies its pre-read status is `pending` or `streaming`. It then runs `UPDATE chat_messages SET status = 'stopped' WHERE id = $1 AND status IN ('streaming','pending')`, but unlike `complete_session()` and `archive_session()` it never checks `rows_affected()`. If the worker completes or errors the message in the gap between the initial read and that update, the guarded update can touch zero rows. The service still logs `"Generation stopped"`, publishes `WsEvent::ChatDone`, and the route still returns `{ stopped: true }`. This is distinct from the already-tracked “no real worker abort” and “publish before commit” problems: even if those are fixed later, the stop API still has a false-success race where nothing was actually transitioned to `stopped`. |

**Desired cleanup**:

  retryable race error when the message is no longer stoppable.

  the compare-and-set update.
- Add regression coverage proving a concurrent completion cannot yield
  `{ stopped: true }` plus `chat.done` when the message never entered
  `stopped`.

### 38.1181 Workspace Settings Update Still Silently Coerces Unrepresentable `maxSpendUsd` Values To `0`

**Status**: Not started  
**Priority**: P2

| Issue | File | Detail |
|-------|------|--------|

On conversion failure, that default is `Decimal::ZERO`, not a validation error. The next spend-check pass then compares current spend against the stored cap with `spend.period_spend >= max_usd`. So an oversized or otherwise unrepresentable spend limit can degrade into a persisted zero-dollar cap and immediately flip the workspace into the same exhausted state as an intentional `0` limit, while the write path still reports success. That is a false-success configuration surface, not just a loose validation edge case. |

**Desired cleanup**:

- Treat `Decimal::try_from(v)` failure as a validation error instead of
  defaulting to `0`.
- Add request-boundary tests covering large but JSON-valid `maxSpendUsd`
  values that exceed the supported decimal range.
- Keep persisted spend-limit semantics aligned with what the caller actually
  sent so bad input cannot silently soft-brick execution.

### 38.1183 Spend History Still Has No Upper Bound On Positive `periods`, So One Request Can Drive Huge Preallocation And N+1 Aggregate Queries

**Status**: Not started  
**Priority**: P2

| Issue | File | Detail |
|-------|------|--------|
| Even after the already-logged negative-value bug, the spend-history endpoint still accepts arbitrarily large positive `periods` values and then preallocates vectors of that size plus runs one aggregate SQL query per period | `generation/g5-api/src/routes/settings.rs:49`, `generation/g5-api/src/routes/settings.rs:61`, `generation/g5-api/src/services/spend_service.rs:464`, `generation/g5-api/src/services/spend_service.rs:488`, `generation/g5-api/src/services/spend_service.rs:505`, `generation/g5-api/src/services/spend_service.rs:507` | `SpendHistoryQueryParams.periods` is just an unconstrained `i32` with a default of `6`; there is no upper-bound validation at the route or service layer. `SpendService::get_spend_history()` immediately reserves two vectors with `Vec::with_capacity(periods as usize)` and then loops over every requested period, issuing a separate `SELECT SUM(...)` query for each boundary pair before also running a final daily-range query. A request such as `?periods=100000` therefore asks the server to allocate large buffers and fan out into 100,000 aggregate queries on one reporting call. That is a performance/availability defect distinct from the signed-cast crash path already logged for negative `periods`: large positive values stay on the “successful” path while still turning a simple dashboard endpoint into a request-amplified load generator. |

**Desired cleanup**:

- Add an explicit upper bound for `periods` at the request boundary and reject
  oversized values with a validation error.
- Replace the per-period query loop with a grouped aggregation strategy so
  normal history requests do not scale linearly in round trips.
- Add load-oriented tests around large positive `periods` values so the API
  contract cannot regress into another reporting DoS path.

**Priority**: P2

|-------|------|--------|

Any `Some(Some(url))` value is copied straight through to `UPDATE users`. That means a direct API caller can save `avatarUrl: ""` or `"   "` as if it were a real avatar. The client then treats that off-contract value as present rather than missing: CRDT awareness publishes `avatarUrl: user?.avatarUrl ?? null`, and the workspace collaborator list falls back to initials only when `p.avatarUrl` is nullish (`p.avatarUrl ?? displayName.charAt(0).toUpperCase()`). A blank string therefore bypasses the fallback path and produces a broken-looking avatar state instead of a sensible initial-based placeholder. This is a backend validation gap that leaks into visible collaboration UI, not just a cosmetic API quirk. |

**Desired cleanup**:

  instead of persisting them as real avatar values.

  before they are stored.
- Add route/service coverage for `""`, whitespace-only, and malformed avatar
  payloads so profile surfaces cannot regress into broken-image state.

### 38.1193 Session Summarization Still Panics On Multi-Byte UTF-8 Titles And Topic Hints
**Status**: ✅ FIXED (synced from `BATCH_PLAN.md`, 2026-04-28)

**Priority**: P2

| Issue | File | Detail |
|-------|------|--------|
| The session-summary heuristics still slice `&str` values at fixed byte offsets (`[..80]` and `[..120]`), so a valid non-ASCII user message can make `summarize_session()` panic when those cut points land inside a UTF-8 codepoint | `generation/g5-api/src/services/chat_service.rs:2098`, `generation/g5-api/src/services/chat_service.rs:2104`, `generation/g5-api/src/services/chat_service.rs:2154`, `generation/g5-api/src/services/chat_service.rs:2157`, `generation/g5-api/src/services/chat_service.rs:2160`, `generation/g5-api/src/routes/chat.rs:1027` | `generate_session_title()` computes `&cleaned[..sentence_end.min(80)]`, and `generate_session_summary()` truncates the topic hint with `&cleaned[..120]`. In Rust, `&str` indices are byte offsets that must fall on character boundaries. So a chat whose first user message contains emoji, accented text, CJK, or any other multibyte UTF-8 can make the summarize endpoint panic purely because the 80-byte or 120-byte cutoff lands in the middle of a codepoint. This is separate from the already-logged stale-summary heuristic issue: even before the content-quality questions, the summarization path is still not safe on perfectly valid Unicode input. |

**Desired cleanup**:

- Truncate session-title and topic-hint text on UTF-8 character boundaries
  instead of slicing raw byte offsets.
- Add regression coverage with multibyte chat content longer than the current
  cutoff lengths so summarize cannot panic on valid Unicode text.
- Reuse the existing safe-truncation patterns already adopted elsewhere in the
  codebase for similar UTF-8 boundary fixes.

So even if a user successfully customizes their profile through `PATCH /api/v1/users/me`, the next OAuth login can silently replace those edits with whatever the provider currently reports. **Desired cleanup**:

  survives a subsequent OAuth login unless the product explicitly intends the
  provider to win.

**Status**: Not started

| Issue | File | Detail |
|-------|------|--------|
| The dedicated session-search route exposes page/per-page pagination, but the query still applies `LIMIT/OFFSET` to `ORDER BY ts_rank_cd(...) DESC, updated_at DESC` with no final stable tiebreaker, so tied rows can move across page boundaries between requests | `generation/g5-api/src/routes/chat.rs:592`, `generation/g5-api/src/routes/chat.rs:607`, `generation/g5-api/src/routes/chat.rs:623`, `generation/g5-api/src/services/chat_service.rs:1193`, `generation/g5-api/src/services/chat_service.rs:1216`, `generation/g5-api/src/services/chat_service.rs:1222` | `search_sessions()` returns paginated results for `/api/v1/workspaces/:workspaceId/sessions/search`, but it sorts only by relevance score and `updated_at` before applying `LIMIT`/`OFFSET`. When two sessions have the same `ts_rank_cd(...)` result and the same `updated_at` timestamp, Postgres is free to return those ties in either order on different reads. This is separate from the already-logged missing query validation issue: even valid session-search queries still do not have a deterministic pagination contract once ties occur. |

**Desired cleanup**:

  ordering, or move the endpoint to cursor/keyset pagination.

But the implementation always returns `Ok(Json(response))`, with the response body using only `"healthy"` or `"degraded"` regardless of which subsystem failed. A dead database, dead search backend, or dead Redis all still produce HTTP 200, and the shared client type even advertises a third `"unhealthy"` state that the route never emits. ### 38.1201 User-Scoped Worker Registration Still Fails Open Against Current Access Rights
**Status**: ✅ FIXED (synced from `BATCH_PLAN.md`, 2026-04-28)

**Priority**: P2

| Issue | File | Detail |
|-------|------|--------|
| User-scoped worker tokens still validate only hash/revocation/expiry at registration time, so a token whose owner no longer has live org membership, `jobs:execute`, or workspace access can still register a worker successfully and only “fail” later by never receiving work | `generation/g5-api/src/services/worker_token_service.rs:306`, `generation/g5-api/src/services/worker_token_service.rs:339`, `generation/g5-api/src/services/task_service.rs:368`, `generation/g5-api/src/services/task_service.rs:425`, `generation/g5-api/src/services/task_service.rs:449`, `generation/g5-api/src/services/task_service.rs:451`, `generation/g5-api/src/services/task_service.rs:529`, `generation/g5-api/src/services/task_service.rs:3794`, `generation/g5-api/src/services/task_service.rs:3806`, `generation/g5-api/src/services/task_service.rs:3826` | `validate_registration_token()` only proves that the secret exists and is not expired or revoked; it does not re-check that `user_id` on a user-scoped token is still an org member or still holds `jobs:execute`. `register_worker()` likewise accepts any requested workspace in the org and inserts an idle worker row without verifying that the token owner can actually access or execute in that workspace. The live permission check only happens later in `poll_for_task()`, where user-scoped workers are narrowed through `executable_workspace_ids_for_user()` / `user_can_execute_workspace()` and simply return `Ok(None)` when the owner has lost access. That turns revoked or mismatched user authority into a false-success bootstrap: worker registration returns `200 OK`, the worker can keep heartbeating, but it will sit idle forever with no explicit explanation that the owner no longer has usable execution rights. |

**Desired cleanup**:

- Re-check live org membership and effective `jobs:execute` rights when
  registering user-scoped workers instead of treating token possession as
  sufficient.
- If `workspace_id` is supplied on a user-scoped registration, validate that
  the owner can actually access and execute in that workspace before inserting
  the worker row.
- Return a structured authorization/validation failure at registration time so
  stale user-scoped tokens do not degrade into confusing “healthy but never
  claims work” workers.

### 38.1202 Worker Capability Parsing Still Broadens Malformed Input To Full Scheduler Access
**Status**: ✅ FIXED (synced from `BATCH_PLAN.md`, 2026-04-28)

**Priority**: P2

| Issue | File | Detail |
|-------|------|--------|
| The worker capability contract still fail-opens: malformed or unrecognized capability lists are accepted at registration and later mapped to **all** worker job types instead of being rejected or narrowed | `generation/g5-common/src/internal_api/dtos.rs:70`, `generation/g5-common/src/internal_api/dtos.rs:72`, `generation/g5-common/src/internal_api/dtos.rs:622`, `generation/g5-api/src/services/task_service.rs:117`, `generation/g5-api/src/services/task_service.rs:118`, `generation/g5-api/src/services/task_service.rs:143`, `generation/g5-api/src/services/task_service.rs:147`, `generation/g5-api/src/services/task_service.rs:358`, `generation/g5-api/src/services/task_service.rs:520` | `RegisterWorkerRequest.capabilities` is documented and tested with examples like `["analysis", "uplift", "downlift"]`, but the scheduler-side parser only recognizes `chat`, `uplift`, `downlift`, `compile`, `test`, `review`, and `custom`. Unknown strings are silently ignored, and if nothing recognized remains, `allowed_job_types_for_worker_capabilities()` falls back to `all_worker_job_types()`. That means a worker registered with `["analysis"]`, `["bogus"]`, or even a non-array JSON value stored in `workers.capabilities` does not get rejected and does not get zero capability. It becomes eligible for every scheduler job type. This is the opposite of fail-closed capability enforcement: typoed, legacy, or malformed capability input broadens the worker’s claim surface instead of constraining it. |

**Desired cleanup**:

- Validate `RegisterWorkerRequest.capabilities` against the supported
  capability vocabulary at registration time and reject unknown entries.
- Decide on an explicit contract for empty capability lists; do not silently
  expand them to full scheduler access.
- Keep the request DTO docs/tests aligned with the real recognized capability
  set so examples like `"analysis"` cannot imply a restriction the scheduler
  does not honor.

### 38.1204 Worker Registration Still Lets `maxConcurrentTasks = 0` Fall Through To A Generic 500
**Status**: ✅ FIXED (synced from `BATCH_PLAN.md`, 2026-04-28)

**Priority**: P3

| Issue | File | Detail |
|-------|------|--------|
| The internal worker-registration contract still accepts `maxConcurrentTasks` as an unconstrained `u32`, but the server does not validate the lower bound before insert, so `0` reaches the database `CHECK` and comes back as a generic internal error instead of a validation failure | `generation/g5-common/src/internal_api/dtos.rs:70`, `generation/g5-common/src/internal_api/dtos.rs:74`, `generation/g5-api/src/services/task_service.rs:345`, `generation/g5-api/src/services/task_service.rs:451`, `generation/g5-api/src/db/migrations/001_initial_schema.sql:671`, `generation/g5-api/src/db/migrations/001_initial_schema.sql:672`, `generation/g5-common/src/error.rs:327` | `RegisterWorkerRequest.max_concurrent_tasks` is just a `u32`, so the raw API accepts `0` as syntactically valid input. `TaskService::register_worker()` does not perform the same `>= 1` check that the workspace settings path already has; it inserts the value directly into `workers.max_concurrent_tasks`. The table schema does enforce `CHECK (max_concurrent_tasks >= 1)`, but that protection sits too late in the stack: the SQLx constraint failure is still converted by the shared error mapping into `G5Error::Internal`. So a caller registering a worker with `maxConcurrentTasks: 0` does not receive a clean `VALIDATION_ERROR` explaining the contract. It gets an opaque 500-level failure even though this is ordinary bad input. This is distinct from the already logged overflow issue: there the value is accepted and silently bricks the worker after storage; here the lower-bound invariant exists in the database, but the API still exposes it as an internal server error instead of input validation. |

**Desired cleanup**:

- Validate `maxConcurrentTasks >= 1` in `register_worker()` before issuing the
  insert, matching the product’s other concurrency-setting paths.
- Keep the internal DTO docs/examples honest about the lower bound instead of
  leaving it to the database schema to enforce implicitly.

But once two rows share the same active/non-active bucket and the same `updated_at` timestamp, Postgres is free to return those ties in either order on different reads because there is no final tiebreaker such as `id DESC`. That makes later pages unstable: a refetch can duplicate a session that already appeared on page N or skip one that should have landed on page N+1. This is distinct from the already-logged filter-validation and workspace-ID issues on the same route: even valid list requests against a real workspace still do not have a deterministic pagination contract once ordering ties occur. |

**Desired cleanup**:

  ordering, or move the endpoint to cursor/keyset pagination.
- Add route/service coverage that exercises equal-status/equal-`updated_at`
  rows across adjacent pages so duplicate/skip behavior cannot regress.

### 38.1209 Internal Worker Lifecycle Routes Still Assume UUID Worker IDs
**Status**: ✅ FIXED (synced from `BATCH_PLAN.md`, 2026-04-28)

**Priority**: P3

| Issue | File | Detail |
|-------|------|--------|
| The shared worker model and JWT/session plumbing still treat `worker_id` as an arbitrary string, but the internal lifecycle routes (`poll`, `claim`, `heartbeat`, `terminate`, `inbox-ws`) still parse the path and auth worker identity as UUIDs, so any non-UUID worker ID becomes unusable after registration | `generation/g5-api/src/models/worker.rs:16`, `generation/g5-api/src/routes/workers.rs:54`, `generation/g5-common/src/auth/minter.rs:76`, `generation/g5-api/src/middleware/auth_middleware.rs:72`, `generation/g5-api/src/routes/internal.rs:56`, `generation/g5-api/src/routes/internal.rs:585`, `generation/g5-api/src/routes/internal.rs:608`, `generation/g5-api/src/routes/internal.rs:639`, `generation/g5-api/src/routes/internal.rs:670`, `generation/g5-api/src/routes/internal.rs:1816` | The product’s own worker identity contract is still string-based end to end: `Worker.id` is `TEXT`, the public worker-detail route explicitly says IDs are arbitrary strings, worker session JWTs are minted from `worker_id: &str`, and `AuthContext::Worker` stores `worker_id` as `String`. But the internal worker-control endpoints still extract `Path<Uuid>` and `require_worker_match()` immediately does `worker_id.parse::<Uuid>()`. So if a worker row ever uses a hostname/container-style ID, the control plane breaks before any real lifecycle logic runs: path extraction rejects the request, or the auth guard turns the worker JWT into an internal error because its `sub` is not UUID-shaped. This is separate from the already-logged internal list-route bug: that one hides non-UUID workers from monitoring, while this one makes the actual internal worker lifecycle contract impossible for them to use at all. |

**Desired cleanup**:

- Make the internal worker lifecycle routes accept string worker IDs, matching
  the shared worker model, JWT claims, and public worker APIs.
- Remove UUID parsing from `require_worker_match()` and compare the authenticated
  worker identity against the path parameter in its native string form.
- Add end-to-end coverage with a non-UUID worker ID so registration, poll,
  heartbeat, terminate, and inbox subscription all prove the same ID contract.

### 38.1210 Internal Task Transition Still Lets Same-Org Workers Mutate Unowned Pending/Waiting Tasks
**Status**: ✅ FIXED (synced from `BATCH_PLAN.md`, 2026-04-28)

**Priority**: P1

| Issue | File | Detail |
|-------|------|--------|
| The internal task-transition pipeline still only enforces worker ownership when `tasks.worker_id` is already populated, so same-org workers can mutate another task's `pending`, `blocked`, or `waiting` row by UUID alone, and the `pending -> running` branch does not even claim the task for the caller | `generation/g5-api/src/routes/internal.rs:750`, `generation/g5-api/src/routes/internal.rs:755`, `generation/g5-api/src/routes/internal.rs:786`, `generation/g5-api/src/services/task_service.rs:2285`, `generation/g5-api/src/services/task_service.rs:2288`, `generation/g5-api/src/services/task_service.rs:2305`, `generation/g5-api/src/services/task_service.rs:2310`, `generation/g5-api/src/services/task_service.rs:2311`, `generation/g5-api/src/services/task_service.rs:2312`, `generation/g5-api/src/services/task_service.rs:2313`, `generation/g5-api/src/services/task_service.rs:2400`, `generation/g5-api/src/services/task_service.rs:2405` | Both `/api/internal/tasks/:id/transition` and the `/status` alias pass the caller's worker id into `transition_task()`, but the guard only rejects mismatches when the locked task row already has `worker_id = Some(...)`. Unassigned rows therefore fail open. The allowed transitions still include `pending -> running`, `blocked -> pending`, `waiting -> pending`, and `waiting -> running`, which are exactly the states that often have `worker_id = NULL`. Worse, the `"running"` branch only updates `tasks.status`; it does **not** set `worker_id`, `assigned_at`, or any lease fields. So a same-org worker that learns another task UUID can requeue or “start” that task without owning it, including pushing it into a zombie `running` state that the normal claim/poll path never established. This is a worker-to-worker isolation bug inside the internal control plane, not just a loose state-machine contract. |

**Desired cleanup**:

- Require explicit worker ownership for internal task transitions unless a
  transition is deliberately designed for unassigned rows.
- Remove or harden `pending -> running` / `waiting -> running` on this generic
  route unless the transition atomically claims the task
  (`worker_id`, `assigned_at`, lease fields).
- Add negative coverage proving one same-org worker cannot requeue or start
  another task by UUID alone.

**Status**: ✅ FIXED (synced from `BATCH_PLAN.md`, 2026-04-28)

### 38.1223 Internal Chat Completion Still Accepts Negative Token Totals
**Status**: ✅ FIXED (synced from `BATCH_PLAN.md`, 2026-04-28)

**Priority**: P2

|-------|------|--------|
| The internal chat completion routes still accept signed `inputTokens` / `outputTokens` values and pass them straight into message/session accounting, so a malformed worker can complete a reply successfully while driving chat token totals and estimated cost backwards | `generation/g5-api/src/routes/internal.rs:1106`, `generation/g5-api/src/routes/internal.rs:1204`, `generation/g5-api/src/services/chat_service.rs:1263`, `generation/g5-api/src/services/chat_service.rs:1311`, `generation/g5-api/src/services/chat_service.rs:1342`, `generation/g5-api/src/services/chat_service.rs:1379`, `generation/g5-api/src/db/migrations/001_initial_schema.sql:539`, `generation/g5-api/src/db/migrations/001_initial_schema.sql:582` | Both `POST /api/internal/messages/:id/complete` and `POST /api/internal/sessions/:id/complete-pending` deserialize `CompleteChatMessageRequest` with `Option<i32>` token fields and perform no lower-bound validation. `ChatService::update_message_status()` then writes those signed values directly into `chat_messages.input_tokens` / `output_tokens`, and when the status is `complete` it increments `chat_sessions.total_input_tokens`, `total_output_tokens`, and `total_cost_usd` by the same signed numbers. Because the cost placeholder is computed from `in_tokens` / `out_tokens` as-is, negative token input can also subtract from `total_cost_usd`. The schema has no `CHECK` constraints preventing negative per-message or aggregate token values. So a bad internal caller can get a 200 OK completion response, emit `chat.done`, and still leave the session with impossible negative usage totals or a reduced cost ledger. This is separate from the already-logged “missing token totals” bug: there the normal runtime omits usage entirely, while this path accepts nonsensical negative usage and records it as successful accounting. |

**Desired cleanup**:

- Reject negative `inputTokens` and `outputTokens` on all internal chat
  completion paths before updating any message or session state.
- Add database constraints so `chat_messages` and `chat_sessions` cannot store
  negative token totals even if another code path bypasses the route checks.
- Add regression coverage proving malformed negative chat token totals fail
  validation instead of decrementing session usage and cost.

**Status**: Not started

| Issue | File | Detail |
